title: CA OAH DDS (Lanterman Act) Decision, OAH No. 2026040023
text:
BEFORE THE
DEPARTMENT OF DEVELOPMENTAL SERVICES
STATE OF CALIFORNIA
In the Matter of:
Claimant OAH Case Nos. 2026040023 & 2026040024
Vs. DECISION BY THE DIRECTOR
Alta California Regional Center
Respondent.
ORDER OF DECISION
On May 28, 2026, an Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) at the Office of Administrative Hearings
(OAH) issued a Proposed Decision in this matter.
The Department of Developmental Services (Department) takes the following action on the attached
Proposed Decision of the ALJ:
The Proposed Decision is adopted by the Department as its Decision in this matter. The Order of
Decision, together with the Proposed Decision, constitute the Decision in this matter.
This is the final administrative Decision. Each party is bound by this Decision. Either party may
request a reconsideration pursuant to Welfare and Institutions Code section 4713, subdivision (b),
within 15 days of receiving the Decision or appeal the Decision to a court of competent jurisdiction
within 180 days of receiving the final Decision.
Attached is a fact sheet with information about what to do and expect after you receive this
decision, and where to get help.
IT IS SO ORDERED on this day June 16, 2026.
Original signed by
Katie Hornberger, Deputy Director
Community Assistance and Resolutions Division

BEFORE THE
DEPARTMENT OF DEVELOPMENTAL SERVICES
STATE OF CALIFORNIA
In the Consolidated Matters of:
CLAIMANT
and
ALTA CALIFORNIA REGIONAL CENTER, Service Agency
DDS Nos. CS0035109 and CS0035141
OAH Nos. 2026040023 and 2026040024
PROPOSED DECISION
Administrative Law Judge Sean Gavin, a Fair Hearing Officer employed by the
Office of Administrative Hearings (OAH), State of California, heard this matter on April
29 and May 26, 2026, by videoconference from Sacramento, CA.
Claimant’s brother represents claimant, who was briefly present at the hearing.
Jordan Cody, J.D., Legal Services Manager, represents Alta California Regional
Center (ACRC). Neither representative is a licensed attorney.
The fair hearing in this matter began on April 29, 2026, but did not conclude.
The hearing officer continued the hearing until May 15, 2026, at 9:00 a.m. The parties
appeared on that day and time and requested a mediation. The matter did not resolve

during the mediation. The parties requested to continue the matter until May 26, 2026,
to allow for additional negotiations.
On May 26, 2026, the parties resolved the matter by Stipulation. They submitted
the Stipulation as Claimant’s Exhibit 34. The Stipulation includes five attachments: (A)
claimant’s Self-Determination Program (SDP) budget for April 1 through May 31, 2026;
(B) claimant’s SDP spending plan for April 1 through May 31, 2026; (C) claimant’s SDP
budget for June 1, 2026, through May 30, 2027; (D) claimant’s SDP spending plan for
June 1, 2026, through May 30, 2027; and (E) claimant's Individual Program Plan (IPP)
for May 31, 2026, through June 1, 2027.
The parties requested that the hearing officer approve the Stipulation, prepare
this Proposed Decision, and submit the Proposed Decision to the Department of
Developmental Services (DDS) for review. The parties submitted the matter for
decision on May 26, 2026.
FACTUAL FINDINGS
Jurisdictional Matters
1. Claimant is a 60-year-old ACRC consumer based on disabilities following
a brain infection in his adolescence. According to his 2026 IPP, “[claimant] does not
want to be institutionalized. [Claimant] wants to continue to live safely at home,
supported by round-the-clock caregiving services and supports which he will purchase
using his SDP budget. This includes community access, and the transportation
required to engage in these activities.” Claimant also wants to attend a day program
when able and would like to receive transportation services to and from the program.
2

2. Since October 2021, claimant has been enrolled in the SDP, which
provides “an individual budget, increased flexibility and choice, and greater control
over decisions, resources, and needed and desired services and supports to
implement” claimant’s Individual Program Plan (IPP). (Welf. & Inst. Code, § 4685.8,
subd. (a).) Various statutes and regulations govern what supports and services a
regional center may fund through the SDP.
ACRC’s Notice of Action and Claimant’s Appeals
3. On March 13, 2026, ACRC issued claimant a Notice of Action (NOA) that
included the following proposed action:
[ACRC] proposes to deny funding for the following services
in the consumer's Self-Determination Program (SDP)
individual budget for the 2026-2027 plan year:
M.O.R.E. Adult Day Program [,] Supportive Living Services
(SLS)[.] These services are denied because ACRC cannot
determine the consumer’s current need for the services due
to insufficient documentation necessary to assess whether
the services remain necessary to implement the consumer's
Individual Program Plan (IPP).
4. On March 20, 2026, claimant appealed the NOA. Claimant stated the
reason for the appeal as follows:
The Self-Determination Program (SDP) and Supported
Living Services (SLS) are substantially different programs.
Under SLS a regional center makes expenditure decisions;
3

whereas, in SDP they do not. Eighteen examples of this
difference are provided in Attachment 01.
Alta has admitted to [claimant’s] representative they run the
SDP program using SLS rules. That is what we are dealing
with here. [Claimant] has, for many years, used his SDP
funding to purchase day program services. Now, after many
years, Alta wants to decide if this purchase is beneficial to
[claimant] (NOA, Att. 02). Because [claimant] is in the SDP
program, Alta lacks the authority to make this decision for
[claimant].
The Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution (Article IV,
CI. 2) insures [sic] the requirements established in the
federal contract which funds the SDP program supersede
any regional center rule. The contract grants expenditure
decision making to the SDP participant, and does not give a
regional center veto power, else [sic] the program would
not be “self-determination.” Alta's effort to invade
[claimant’s] rights under SDP defies the intention of the
federal government, which is that the consumer “self-
determine.”
Respectfully, the court must find Alta's NOA to be null and
void.
5. Additionally, on March 19, 2026, claimant submitted a separate appeal
form but checked a box indicating he was not appealing an NOA or a Good Faith
4

Belief Letter. Rather, claimant characterized his “reason(s) for appeal” as “Emergency
Order Requested” and wrote:
FACTS NOT IN DISPUTE: [Claimant] is a developmentally
disabled person (DDP) and long time Lanterman Act
beneficiary. [Claimant]is not safe alone in public, cannot
handle his affairs, cannot safely cook or take medication. He
requires 24 hour per day protective caregiving. In 2022
Alta's attorneys settled a case by enrolling [Claimant] in
SDP. [Claimant’s] brother has operated [claimant’s] SDP
business ever since, employing three full time caregivers.
Monthly, [claimant] receives 283 hours of IHSS [In Home
Supportive Services] protective supervision funding. The
remaining 447.5 hours are paid by [Claimant] using his SDP
funding.
SDP BUDGET & SPENDING PLAN EXPIRE IN 12 DAYS:
[Claimant’s] current SDP budget and spending plan expire
March 31, 2026. If these are not renewed, on April 01 2026
[claimant] will no longer have the funds to pay his
caregivers and he will have to furlough them. That will leave
[claimant] alone and may prove fatal. It will also devastate
the finances of two of his caregivers, who may have to seek
other employment. One has been with [claimant] almost
four years.
ALTA IS NOT RESPONDING TO REQUESTS TO RENEW:
Anticipating the need to renew his annual SDP budget and
5

spending plan, on four occasions between January 28 and
March 16, 2026. [claimant] emailed Alta requesting renewal
(Att. 1-4). No response was received. In prior case sworn
testimony, and in email obtained by subpoena, senior Alta
leaders admitted they do not respond to email from
[claimant’s] representative (Att. 5-7). This is happening
again. It may be that Alta is retaliating because recently
[claimant] declined to waive some of his rights under the
SDP program.
EMERGENCY ORDER REQUESTED: It is respectfully
requested the court expeditiously order Alta to renew
[claimant’s] SDP budget and spending plan at their current
rates.
6. Upon ACRC’s request, OAH consolidated the appeals for hearing. The
matter then proceeded and resolved by Stipulation as described above.
LEGAL CONCLUSIONS
1. When a regional center decides to reduce, terminate, or change services
set forth in an IPP, it must notify the recipient of those services in writing on a form
prescribed by DDS. (Welf. & Inst. Code, §§ 4701, subd. (a), 4710, subd. (a)(1).) A
recipient of services who is dissatisfied with a decision or action of a regional center
may appeal by requesting an informal meeting, a mediation, and/or a fair hearing. (Id.
at § 4710.5, subd. (a).)
6

2. For matters involving the SDP, within 10 days of the hearing’s conclusion,
the hearing officer must render a proposed decision for DDS’s review. (Welf. & Inst.
Code, § 4712.5, subd. (a)(2).) Within 30 days of receiving the proposed decision, DDS
may adopt the proposed decision as written or decide the matter on the record,
including the recording, with or without taking additional evidence. (Id. at subd. (e)(2).)
3. ACRC timely and properly notified claimant of its proposed change to his
SDP budget pursuant to Welfare and Institutions Code sections 4701, subdivision (a),
and 4710, subdivision (a)(1). Claimant timely and properly appealed pursuant to
Welfare and Institutions Code section 4710.5, subdivision (a).
4. The parties’ Stipulation fully addresses all issues raised in ACRC’s NOA
and claimant’s appeals. Consequently, as described in the Stipulation, the parties shall
adopt and follow: (1) claimant’s SDP budget for April 1 through May 31, 2026; (2)
claimant’s SDP spending plan for April 1 through May 31, 2026; (3) claimant’s SDP
budget for June 1, 2026, through May 30, 2027; (4) claimant’s SDP spending plan for
June 1, 2026, through May 30, 2027; and (5) claimant's IPP for May 31, 2026, through
June 1, 2027.

ORDER
This matter having been resolved by Stipulation of the parties, the Stipulation is
approved, and the parties are ordered to adopt and follow: (1) claimant’s SDP budget
for April 1 through May 31, 2026; (2) claimant’s SDP spending plan for April 1 through
May 31, 2026; (3) claimant’s SDP budget for June 1, 2026, through May 30, 2027; (4)
claimant’s SDP spending plan for June 1, 2026, through May 30, 2027; and (5)
claimant's IPP for May 31, 2026, through June 1, 2027.
